analysis.one_liner: Makes foreign oil cartels like OPEC subject to US antitrust lawsuits.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a committee hearing or a House vote and expired when the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would declare it illegal under US antitrust law for foreign states to band together to limit oil and gas production or fix prices. It would strip foreign governments of their usual shield from US courts (sovereign immunity) in these cases and let the Attorney General sue them directly. The aim is to break up production coordination by oil-exporting cartels, which raises prices at the pump for American consumers.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary consumers, especially drivers and businesses that depend on fuel, would benefit if coordinated output cuts by foreign oil states became legally risky and gas prices stayed lower than they otherwise would.

how_it_helps.text: The bill makes it illegal for foreign states to act collectively to limit oil production, set oil prices, or restrain trade in oil, natural gas, or other petroleum products when those actions affect the US market [S2].
It removes sovereign immunity and act-of-state defenses in these cases, so foreign governments could actually be sued and have judgments enforced against them in US courts [S2].
The bill gives the Attorney General sole authority to bring enforcement actions in federal district court under the antitrust laws [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Foreign oil-producing states, including OPEC members and their national oil companies, would face antitrust liability and damage judgments. US oil and gas producers would earn less if coordinated production cuts were blocked and prices fell.
analysis.who_pays_short: OPEC states and US oil producers

drawbacks.text: Applying US antitrust law to foreign sovereigns' own production decisions is an extraordinary step that risks retaliation against US companies and complicates diplomatic relations with major oil producers like Saudi Arabia [S2].

Only the Attorney General could bring a case [S3], so enforcement would depend entirely on the political priorities of whatever administration is in power — and any administration may hesitate to sue a country it relies on diplomatically.

Even a successful lawsuit may not lower prices much in the short run, since world oil prices depend on many factors beyond cartel coordination, and litigation against sovereign states could take years.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For American consumers, the upside is real: a legal tool to challenge foreign oil states that coordinate to keep supply tight and prices high. The costs fall mostly on foreign oil producers and, to a lesser extent, US producers through lower prices. The main design weakness is that enforcement rests solely with the Attorney General, making the tool only as strong as the administration's willingness to use it against diplomatically sensitive partners.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the House Judiciary Committee, which never took it up, and it died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Ken Buck introduced the bill on May 5, 2023, joined by Reps. Jerrold Nadler and David Cicilline, who were recorded as cosponsors [S1].
The same day, the bill was referred to the House Committee on the Judiciary [S5].
No further action appears in the bill's record — no hearings, markup, or vote — and the bill expired at the end of the 118th Congress on January 3, 2025 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Foreign oil-producing states and their national oil companies came out ahead: they keep the ability to coordinate production and pricing without facing US antitrust suits, and consumers got no new tool to challenge those arrangements.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Foreign oil-exporting cartels and US oil producers

industries.industry: Foreign state oil producers (OPEC and similar cartels)
industries.note: These states coordinate to limit production and support prices; the bill would let the US government sue them for it and strip their sovereign immunity shield in court. Their loss would be consumers' gain at the pump.
Blocking foreign coordinated output cuts would tend to lower world prices, cutting into US producer revenue. Their interest in the bill's failure ran against consumers seeking cheaper fuel.
